transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. It is really nice to meet you, and thank you so much for fitting me in. I hope I'm not taking up too much of your time. 

I'm... well, I'm just here because I want to make sure I'm doing everything right, you know? I've been having this little issue at work—I'm a nursing assistant—and I really hope this doesn't sound terrible or make you think poorly of me. But... I keep hearing these voices. They come through the call-light speaker at the station, and sometimes from the hallway vents. They keep telling me which patient records have been changed. 

It's just... it's as clear as somebody standing right next to me. But even when the unit is completely quiet, nobody else seems to hear it but me. Does... does that make sense? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information and explaining it okay.
Can you tell me if these voices happen every day, or do they come and go? Also, have you noticed any other experiences where you see, hear, or believe something that others don’t seem to share?

Oh, um, the voices... they mostly come and go. It seems to happen the most when I'm on my shift. I hope that answers that part okay. 

As for other things... gosh, I really don't want you to think I'm a difficult employee or a troublemaker, because I really do love my job and I always try my absolute best. But... well, I've noticed something with the wound-care charts. There's this pattern in them, and... I just know management doesn't want anyone to see it. 

I did mention it to my supervisor, just trying to be helpful and do the right thing, you know? She told me it was just late entries or some coding mistakes. But... I can just tell they're watching what I write in the system now. Because I'm the one who caught the pattern. 

I'm so sorry, I know that probably sounds terrible, or maybe a little paranoid? I just want to make sure I'm giving you all the details you need and being completely honest. Am I explaining this okay for you?

Can you tell me more about your belief that management is watching what you write in the system? Do you believe they are doing this because they think you are a threat or because they are trying to hide something?

Oh, well... I really hope I don't sound like I'm accusing my bosses of anything malicious. I respect them so much, and I always try to be a good team player. But... yes, I suppose I do think they're trying to hide it. 

I just know those wound-care charts are showing a pattern that management absolutely doesn't want anyone to see. And even though my supervisor was very polite when she told me it was just late entries or coding mistakes... I can just tell. I smiled and nodded at work because I didn't want to be difficult, but... they're watching what I write in the system specifically because I'm the one who caught it. I think they just want to monitor my notes to make sure I don't document anything about the pattern, you know? 

I really hate even thinking these things about them, but I just know what I saw. I hope I'm not overstepping or sounding too negative by saying all this out loud. Does that help answer your question, Doctor?
Have there ever been times—maybe lasting several months or more—when these experiences, like hearing voices or believing that management is hiding something, weren’t happening at all?

Oh, um, yes... yes, absolutely. I never used to have these experiences at all. I really want to be clear about that, because I don't want you to think I've always struggled with my work or that I'm normally a suspicious person. For years and years, everything was completely fine. 

None of this—the voices from the call-light speaker, or noticing those patterns in the charts—none of it happened until recently. It really only started during this time when... well, when I got so incredibly wound up and driven about the new rollout at the facility. 

I was just... I felt so certain that I had to fix everything and make it all perfect, you know? I wanted to be the best employee I could be. I started sleeping a lot less, and I was just working nonstop, practically buzzing with all this energy to get things done. And it was only after I got into that state—working so hard and barely sleeping—that the voices and the chart things started happening. 

I hope that makes sense? I just want to reassure you that this isn't how I normally am, and I'm really trying my best to give you the whole picture. Is that the kind of information you were looking for?
Can you tell me if there was ever a time when these experiences, like hearing voices or believing management was hiding something, lasted for a month or more without stopping?

Well, um... I guess it has been going on for a little while now. I really hope it doesn't sound like I've been letting it affect my work for too long, because I always try to push through and be professional. But... yes, I suppose it's been about two months now. 

It all started right around the time they asked me to help lead the new wound-care documentation rollout. I was just so honored they chose me, and I wanted to do such a good job for them. But that's when this all kind of... started up. And it hasn't really stopped since then. 

I'm so sorry if two months sounds like a long time to let this go on without saying anything. I just kept thinking I could handle it and be a good employee. Am I giving you the right timeline, Doctor? Is that what you needed to know?

latest_inference.note: The patient reports that the symptoms (hearing voices and believing management is hiding something) have been ongoing for about two months without stopping, and they occur in the context of a recent high-pressure work situation. This duration and the presence of both hallucinations and delusions support a diagnosis of F23.2 (Acute and Transient Psychotic Disorder) rather than F23.8 (Other Acute Delusional Disorders), which is less specific and typically involves shorter or more fluctuating symptoms.

inference_history.note: The patient's presentation includes persistent, fixed beliefs about management monitoring their charting and a pattern in wound-care charts that others do not acknowledge. There is no clear evidence of prominent hallucinations outside of the described voices related to the records, which may be context-specific or influenced by the delusional framework. This points toward a delusional disorder (F22) or other delusional-like disorders such as F23.2 (persistent delusional disorder), F23.8, or F23.9. Schizophrenia spectrum disorders (e.g., F20.x, F25.x) are less likely given the absence of core Schneiderian first-rank symptoms, disorganization, or negative symptoms. Brief psychotic disorder (F23.0) is ruled out due to the chronic nature of the symptoms.

The patient reported a temporal relationship between the onset of symptoms and a period of increased work effort, reduced sleep, and heightened energy, suggesting a possible brief psychotic disorder (F23.2) or another specified schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder (F23.8). The history of a prior period without symptoms and the relatively short duration of the current episode support this narrowing. Other candidates from the previous list (F22, F23.9) are less consistent with the clinical picture now that more information has been provided.

The patient reports that the symptoms (hearing voices and believing management is hiding something) have been ongoing for about two months without stopping, and they occur in the context of a recent high-pressure work situation. This duration and the presence of both hallucinations and delusions support a diagnosis of F23.2 (Acute and Transient Psychotic Disorder) rather than F23.8 (Other Acute Delusional Disorders), which is less specific and typically involves shorter or more fluctuating symptoms.
